questions.stem: Neither the coach nor the players ____ aware of the change in venue yesterday.

explain.why: 'yesterday' is a finished time, so the present perfect 'has been' cannot be used, and it is singular.
With 'neither ... nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'players', which is plural, so 'was' is wrong.
'yesterday' needs the past tense, and 'is' is also singular while 'players' is plural.

solution: Neither the coach nor the players were aware of the change in venue yesterday.
With 'neither ... nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'players' (plural), and 'yesterday' needs the past tense.

questions.stem: Either Mr Tan or his assistants ____ the answer sheets every Friday.

explain.why: With 'either ... or' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'assistants', which is plural, so the singular 'collects' is wrong.
'every Friday' shows a repeated habit, not a completed action, so the present perfect does not fit.
'every Friday' shows a regular habit, which needs the simple present, and 'is' is singular.

solution: Either Mr Tan or his assistants collect the answer sheets every Friday.
A habit ('every Friday') takes the simple present, and the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'assistants' (plural).

questions.stem: Each of the pupils in Class 6C ____ a copy of the revision notes now.

explain.why: 'have' meaning 'own' is not used in the continuous form, and 'are' is plural.
'Each' is singular, so the plural 'have' is wrong even though 'pupils' comes just before the verb.
'now' shows the present, so the past tense 'had' does not fit.

solution: Each of the pupils in Class 6C has a copy of the revision notes now.
'Each' is singular and 'now' shows the present, so the verb is 'has'.

questions.stem: A number of pupils ____ chosen to represent the school so far.

explain.why: 'A number of' means 'several', so the verb is plural; 'has been' is singular.
'so far' links the past to now, so the simple past 'was' does not fit.
'so far' needs the present perfect, and 'is' is singular while 'a number of pupils' means several.

solution: A number of pupils have been chosen to represent the school so far.
'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb, and 'so far' needs the present perfect: 'have been'.

questions.stem: The number of pupils who take the bus to school ____ risen steadily since 2020.

explain.why: 'since 2020' needs the present perfect, so 'is' cannot be used with 'risen'.
'since 2020' needs the present perfect, so 'was' cannot be used with 'risen'.
The subject is 'the number', which is singular, so 'have' is wrong even though 'pupils' is nearby.

solution: The number of pupils who take the bus to school has risen steadily since 2020.
'The number of' is singular and 'since 2020' needs the present perfect: 'has risen'.

questions.stem: The box of colour pencils that Auntie Mei gave my sisters ____ missing from the cupboard.

explain.why: The subject 'the box' is singular, so the plural 'were' is wrong.
The subject is 'the box', which is singular; 'pencils' and 'sisters' are inside the describing phrases.
'have been' is plural, but the subject 'the box' is singular.

solution: The box of colour pencils that Auntie Mei gave my sisters is missing from the cupboard.
The subject is 'the box', which is singular, so the verb is 'is'.

questions.stem: Everyone except the two monitors ____ allowed to leave the hall early yesterday.

explain.why: 'yesterday' needs the past tense, and 'are' is also plural.
'yesterday' needs the past tense, so the present 'is' is wrong.
'Everyone' is singular, and the phrase 'except the two monitors' does not change that.

solution: Everyone except the two monitors was allowed to leave the hall early yesterday.
'Everyone' is singular and 'yesterday' needs the past: 'was'.

questions.stem: One of the stalls at the bazaar ____ pineapple tarts at half price last Saturday.

explain.why: 'last Saturday' is in the past, so the base form 'sell' is wrong.
'last Saturday' is a finished time, so the present perfect 'has sold' cannot be used.
'One' is the subject and it is singular, so the plural 'were' is wrong.

solution: One of the stalls at the bazaar sold pineapple tarts at half price last Saturday.
The subject is 'one', and 'last Saturday' needs the simple past: 'sold'.

questions.stem: The teacher, together with her pupils, ____ planting trees at Pasir Ris Park yesterday morning.

explain.why: 'together with her pupils' does not make the subject plural; the subject is 'the teacher'.
'yesterday morning' needs the past tense, and 'are' is also plural.
'yesterday morning' needs the past tense, so 'is' is wrong.

solution: The teacher, together with her pupils, was planting trees at Pasir Ris Park yesterday morning.
'Together with ...' does not change the subject 'the teacher' (singular), and 'yesterday' needs the past: 'was'.

questions.stem: Half of the pupils in my class ____ spectacles.

explain.why: 'is' is singular, but 'half of the pupils' is plural.
'Half of the pupils' refers to several pupils, so the verb is plural.
The sentence states what they usually do, which needs the simple present, and 'has' is singular.

solution: Half of the pupils in my class wear spectacles.
'Half of the pupils' is plural, and a general fact takes the simple present: 'wear'.

questions.stem: By the time the bus reached the stop, the rain ____ for ten minutes and the pupils were drenched.

explain.why: 'By the time the bus reached' is in the past, so the present perfect continuous does not fit.
'for ten minutes' before another past event needs a perfect form, not the simple past 'fell'.
The sentence is about the past ('reached', 'were drenched'), so 'is falling' is wrong.

solution: By the time the bus reached the stop, the rain had been falling for ten minutes and the pupils were drenched.
'For ten minutes' before a past event needs the past perfect continuous: 'had been falling'.

questions.stem: Mei Ling opened the door and ____ that someone had left a parcel on the doorstep.

explain.why: The past perfect is for an action before another past action, but seeing came after opening the door.
'opened' and 'had left' are past, so the present 'sees' breaks the tense.
The present perfect 'has seen' does not match the past narrative in 'opened'.

solution: Mei Ling opened the door and saw that someone had left a parcel on the doorstep.
Both actions happened in order in the past, so the simple past 'saw' is used.

questions.stem: While the teacher was explaining the answer, a few pupils ____ whispering at the back of the class.

explain.why: 'a few pupils' is plural, so 'was' is wrong.
'was explaining' is past, so the present 'are' breaks the tense.
The present perfect does not match the past continuous 'was explaining'.

solution: While the teacher was explaining the answer, a few pupils were whispering at the back of the class.
'A few pupils' is plural and the sentence is in the past continuous: 'were whispering'.

questions.stem: The Science Fair, which ____ every year since 2015, will be held at the school hall next month.

explain.why: 'since 2015' needs the present perfect, not the simple present.
The past perfect is for an event before a past time, but the Fair is still held now.
'since 2015' needs the present perfect; the simple past does not link the past to now.

solution: The Science Fair, which has been held every year since 2015, will be held at the school hall next month.
'Since 2015' needs the present perfect: 'has been held'.

questions.stem: I ____ for my turn at the clinic for an hour when the nurse finally called my name.

explain.why: 'called' is past, so the present perfect continuous does not fit.
The nurse 'called' my name in the past, so 'am waiting' is wrong.
The sentence is in the past, so the simple present 'wait' is wrong.

solution: I had been waiting for my turn at the clinic for an hour when the nurse finally called my name.
The waiting lasted an hour before the past event 'called', so the past perfect continuous 'had been waiting' is needed.

questions.stem: My family ____ to Sentosa three times so far this year, and we plan another trip in December.

explain.why: The past perfect is for something before another past time, but this period continues to now.
'so far this year' links the past to now, so the simple past 'went' does not fit.
'was' cannot show visits made up to now; 'so far this year' needs the present perfect.

solution: My family has been to Sentosa three times so far this year, and we plan another trip in December.
'So far this year' needs the present perfect: 'has been'.

questions.stem: I will call you as soon as I ____ at the hotel.

explain.why: The call is in the future, so the past tense 'arrived' is wrong.
A time clause with 'as soon as' uses the simple present, not the continuous.
After 'as soon as' a time clause uses the simple present, not 'will'.

solution: I will call you as soon as I arrive at the hotel.
A time clause about the future uses the simple present: 'as soon as I arrive'.

questions.stem: Tomorrow, after the pupils ____ their art work, they will clean the art room.

explain.why: A time clause after 'after' uses the simple present; the continuous does not fit.
After 'after' a time clause uses the simple present, not 'will'.
'Tomorrow' is in the future, so the past tense is wrong.

solution: Tomorrow, after the pupils finish their art work, they will clean the art room.
A future time clause with 'after' uses the simple present: 'after the pupils finish'.

questions.stem: Ravi ____ the same pair of shoes since he was in Primary 4, and they are now too small.

explain.why: The past perfect is for an action before another past time, but he still wears them now.
'since' with a period up to now needs the present perfect, not the simple past.
'since he was in Primary 4' needs the present perfect, not the present continuous.

solution: Ravi has worn the same pair of shoes since he was in Primary 4, and they are now too small.
'Since he was in Primary 4' with 'now' needs the present perfect: 'has worn'.

questions.stem: The cat ____ on the sofa when the doorbell rang, but it jumped down and ran away.

explain.why: The sleeping was in progress when the bell interrupted it, so the past continuous is expected.
'rang' is past, so the present perfect does not fit.
'rang' and 'jumped' are past, so 'sleeps' breaks the tense.

solution: The cat was sleeping on the sofa when the doorbell rang, but it jumped down and ran away.
A background action interrupted by 'rang' takes the past continuous: 'was sleeping'.

questions.stem: Please remember that the library ____ at 5 p.m. on weekdays, so return your books before then.

explain.why: The sentence gives a regular opening time for now, not a past event.
The past perfect is for something before another past time, but this is a regular timetable.
'on weekdays' shows a regular schedule, not a completed action.

solution: Please remember that the library closes at 5 p.m. on weekdays, so return your books before then.
A regular timetable takes the simple present: 'closes'.

questions.stem: If the haze ____ worse tomorrow, the school will cancel all outdoor activities.

explain.why: 'got' belongs to an unreal or past condition, but 'will cancel' shows a real future.
The past perfect is for an unreal past condition, which does not match 'will cancel'.
The 'if' clause for a likely future event uses the simple present, not 'will'.

solution: If the haze gets worse tomorrow, the school will cancel all outdoor activities.
A real future condition uses the simple present in the 'if' clause and 'will' in the main clause.

questions.stem: If Ethan ____ the top prize in the lucky draw, he would buy a new bicycle for his brother.

explain.why: 'would buy' shows an unlikely situation, so the 'if' clause needs the past, not the present.
'will' is not used in an 'if' clause.
The past perfect goes with 'would have bought', not 'would buy'.

solution: If Ethan won the top prize in the lucky draw, he would buy a new bicycle for his brother.
'Would buy' shows an unlikely present or future situation, so the 'if' clause uses the simple past: 'won'.

questions.stem: If the bus driver had not braked so quickly, the pupils ____ injured.

explain.why: The past perfect belongs in the 'if' clause; the result clause needs 'would have been'.
'will have been' is the future perfect; this condition is unreal and in the past.
The 'if' clause is about a past event, so the result needs 'would have' plus the past participle.

solution: If the bus driver had not braked so quickly, the pupils would have been injured.
An unreal past condition ('had not braked') takes 'would have been' in the result clause.

questions.stem: Unless you ____ harder, you will not pass the Chinese oral examination.

explain.why: 'will not pass' shows a real future, so the 'unless' clause needs the simple present.
'will' is not used in an 'unless' clause.
'Unless' already means 'if ... not', so adding 'don't' makes a double negative.

solution: Unless you practise harder, you will not pass the Chinese oral examination.
'Unless' means 'if ... not', so the verb stays positive and in the simple present: 'practise'.

questions.stem: If you ____ the tap properly, the water would not have flooded the toilet.

explain.why: 'would' is not used in an 'if' clause like this.
'would not have flooded' is about the past, so the 'if' clause needs the past perfect.
The present tense 'close' does not fit an unreal past condition.

solution: If you had closed the tap properly, the water would not have flooded the toilet.
An unreal past result ('would not have flooded') needs 'had' plus the past participle in the 'if' clause: 'had closed'.

questions.stem: If the MRT service ____ delayed again tomorrow, many pupils will be late for school.

explain.why: 'will' is not used in an 'if' clause about the future.
'will be late' shows a real future, so the past 'was' does not fit.
'were' is for unreal situations, but 'will be late' shows a real future.

solution: If the MRT service is delayed again tomorrow, many pupils will be late for school.
A real future condition uses the simple present in the 'if' clause: 'is delayed'.

questions.stem: The teacher ____ car was parked outside the gate is our new Art teacher.

explain.why: 'whom' is the object form and cannot show possession.
'which' is for things, and the sentence refers to a person.
'who' stands for the teacher as the subject, but here we need to show the car belongs to the teacher.

solution: The teacher whose car was parked outside the gate is our new Art teacher.
'Whose' shows that the car belongs to the teacher.

questions.stem: My cousin, ____ lives in Tampines, is a lifeguard.

explain.why: 'whose' shows possession, but nothing belongs to the cousin here.
'which' is for things, but 'my cousin' is a person.
'whom' is for the object, but here the pronoun is the subject of 'lives'.

solution: My cousin, who lives in Tampines, is a lifeguard.
The pronoun is the subject of 'lives' and refers to a person, so 'who' is used.

questions.stem: The pupil to ____ the principal presented the trophy is from my class.

explain.why: 'whose' shows possession, but nothing belongs to the pupil here.
After a preposition such as 'to', the object form 'whom' is needed.
'which' is for things, but the sentence refers to a pupil.

solution: The pupil to whom the principal presented the trophy is from my class.
After the preposition 'to', a person takes 'whom'.

questions.stem: This is the same school ____ my father studied thirty years ago.

explain.why: 'who' is for people, but 'school' is a place.
'which' would need a preposition ('in which'), so it does not fit here alone.
'whose' shows possession, but nothing belongs to the school here.

solution: This is the same school where my father studied thirty years ago.
'Where' refers to a place and needs no preposition after it.

questions.stem: Everything ____ the guide told us about the old shophouses was fascinating.

explain.why: 'whom' is for people, but 'everything' is not a person.
'who' is for people, but 'everything' is not a person.
'what' cannot follow 'everything'; 'that' is used to join the clause.

solution: Everything that the guide told us about the old shophouses was fascinating.
After 'everything' the relative pronoun is 'that'.

questions.stem: Ben and I made the poster by ____ without any help from the teacher.

explain.why: The doers are 'Ben and I', two people, so the reflexive must be plural.
'ourself' is not a standard form; the plural is 'ourselves'.
'themselves' refers to other people, but the doers include 'I'.

solution: Ben and I made the poster by ourselves without any help from the teacher.
'Ben and I' is 'we', so the reflexive pronoun is 'ourselves'.

questions.stem: The principal is proud ____ the school's achievements at the National Day parade.

explain.why: 'proud' is followed by 'of', not 'for'.
'proud' is followed by 'of', not 'at'.
'proud' is followed by 'of', not 'with'.

solution: The principal is proud of the school's achievements at the National Day parade.
The adjective 'proud' is followed by 'of'.

questions.stem: Wei Jie is exceptionally good ____ solving difficult Math problems.

explain.why: 'good on' is not used for a skill.
'good for' means beneficial, which does not fit solving problems.
'good to' means kind towards someone, which does not fit here.

solution: Wei Jie is exceptionally good at solving difficult Math problems.
'Good at' is used for a skill followed by an '-ing' form.

questions.stem: The monitors are responsible ____ keeping the classroom clean.

explain.why: 'responsible' is followed by 'for' for a duty.
'responsible' is followed by 'for', not 'at'.
'responsible to' names the person you answer to, not the duty.

solution: The monitors are responsible for keeping the classroom clean.
A duty follows 'responsible for'.

questions.stem: Our neighbour is very fond ____ feeding the stray cats near the void deck.

explain.why: 'fond' is followed by 'of', not 'about'.
'fond' is followed by 'of', not 'with'.
'fond' is followed by 'of', not 'for'.

solution: Our neighbour is very fond of feeding the stray cats near the void deck.
The adjective 'fond' is followed by 'of'.

questions.stem: Many pupils are afraid ____ speaking in front of the whole school.

explain.why: 'afraid' is followed by 'of', not 'at'.
'afraid' is followed by 'of', not 'with'.
'afraid' is followed by 'of', not 'from'.

solution: Many pupils are afraid of speaking in front of the whole school.
The adjective 'afraid' is followed by 'of' plus an '-ing' form.

questions.stem: My brother is allergic ____ prawns.

explain.why: 'allergic' is followed by 'to', not 'of'.
'allergic' is followed by 'to', not 'for'.
'allergic' is followed by 'to', not 'with'.

solution: My brother is allergic to prawns.
The adjective 'allergic' is followed by 'to'.

questions.stem: You may borrow my notes ____ you return them by Friday.

explain.why: 'unless' means 'if not', which reverses the condition.
'although' shows contrast, but returning the notes is a condition.
'as though' compares with an imagined situation; it does not set a condition.

solution: You may borrow my notes provided that you return them by Friday.
'Provided that' sets a condition for borrowing the notes.

questions.stem: The match was not cancelled ____ the heavy rain.

explain.why: 'although' must be followed by a clause with a subject and verb, but 'the heavy rain' is only a noun phrase.
'so that' shows purpose and needs a clause.
'because' needs a clause and also gives a reason, but the match went on.

solution: The match was not cancelled despite the heavy rain.
'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase and shows contrast.

questions.stem: Not only did Ken finish his homework early, ____ he also helped his sister with hers.

explain.why: 'so' shows result, but the sentence adds a second point.
'or' offers a choice, but the sentence adds a second point.
'not only' is paired with 'but', not 'and'.

solution: Not only did Ken finish his homework early, but he also helped his sister with hers.
'Not only ... but also' is a paired structure.

questions.stem: The ice cream melted so quickly ____ we could hardly finish it.

explain.why: 'than' is used in comparisons, but 'so quickly' needs a result clause.
'which' is a relative pronoun and does not join a result clause here.
'as' does not complete 'so quickly' to show a result.

solution: The ice cream melted so quickly that we could hardly finish it.
'So ... that' links a cause to its result.

questions.stem: The teacher suggested ____ the excursion to the following week.

explain.why: 'to postponing' mixes an infinitive marker with an '-ing' form.
'suggest' is followed by an '-ing' form, not 'to' plus the verb.
Here 'suggest' needs an '-ing' form, so the base verb is wrong.

solution: The teacher suggested postponing the excursion to the following week.
The verb 'suggest' is followed by an '-ing' form: 'suggested postponing'.

questions.stem: My parents don't allow me ____ video games on weekdays.

explain.why: 'allow someone' needs 'to' plus the base verb, not the past tense.
'allow me' is followed by the 'to' infinitive; '-ing' follows 'allow' only without an object.
'allow someone' needs 'to' before the verb.

solution: My parents don't allow me to play video games on weekdays.
'Allow someone to' is followed by the base verb.

questions.stem: We were looking forward to ____ our grandparents at the airport.

explain.why: 'to be seeing' is not formed correctly after a preposition.
'to' is a preposition here, so the verb must be an '-ing' form.
In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so the verb takes '-ing'.

solution: We were looking forward to seeing our grandparents at the airport.
In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so '-ing' follows.

questions.stem: The little boy taught ____ how to ride a bicycle by watching videos.

explain.why: 'itself' is for things or animals, but the subject is a boy.
'herself' is feminine, but the subject is a boy.
The boy is both the teacher and the learner, so a reflexive pronoun is needed; 'him' would refer to someone else.

solution: The little boy taught himself how to ride a bicycle by watching videos.
The subject and object are the same boy, so the reflexive 'himself' is used.

questions.stem: The window in our classroom ____ by a football yesterday.

explain.why: 'yesterday' is a finished past time, so the present 'is broken' does not fit.
'The window' is singular, so 'were broken' does not agree with it.
'broke' is active, but the window did not do the breaking; the football did, so a passive form is needed.

solution: The window in our classroom was broken by a football yesterday.
The window receives the action and 'yesterday' is past, so use the simple past passive 'was broken' (singular subject).

questions.stem: English ____ in all Singapore schools.

explain.why: 'is teaching' is active, but English is not the one doing the teaching.
'teaches' is active, but English does not teach anyone; it is the subject being taught, so the passive is needed.
'English' is a singular subject, so 'are taught' does not agree.

solution: English is taught in all Singapore schools.
English receives the action and the sentence states a general fact, so use the simple present passive 'is taught'.

questions.stem: The new MRT station ____ by the Prime Minister last week.

explain.why: 'opened' is active, so it cannot be followed by 'by the Prime Minister' naming the doer.
'last week' is past time, so the present 'is opened' does not fit.
'has opened' is active and also clashes with 'last week'; the station was opened by someone.

solution: The new MRT station was opened by the Prime Minister last week.
'by the Prime Minister' names the doer of the action and 'last week' is past, so use the simple past passive 'was opened'.

questions.stem: These cookies ____ by my grandmother every Chinese New Year.

explain.why: 'baked' is active, so it cannot take 'by my grandmother' as the doer.
'These cookies' is plural, so 'is baked' does not agree.
'are baking' is active, so it cannot take 'by my grandmother' as the doer.

solution: These cookies are baked by my grandmother every Chinese New Year.
The cookies receive the action and 'every Chinese New Year' shows a habit, so use the simple present passive 'are baked' (plural subject).

questions.stem: A new playground ____ in our estate next month.

explain.why: 'will build' is active, but a playground cannot build itself; it is built by workers.
'will be building' is active continuous, but the playground is not doing the building.
'next month' is future, so the present perfect passive 'has been built' does not fit.

solution: A new playground will be built in our estate next month.
The playground receives the action and 'next month' is future, so use the future passive 'will be built'.

questions.stem: My bicycle ____ from the void deck, so I reported it to the police.

explain.why: 'had stolen' is active, so it would mean the bicycle was the thief.
'was stealing' is active, and the bicycle is not the thief.
'stole' is active, but the bicycle did not steal anything; it was taken from the owner.

solution: My bicycle was stolen from the void deck, so I reported it to the police.
The bicycle receives the action of stealing, so use the simple past passive 'was stolen'.

questions.stem: Rice ____ by farmers in many parts of Asia.

explain.why: 'Rice' is an uncountable, singular subject, so 'are grown' does not agree.
'grows' is active, so it cannot be followed by 'by farmers' naming the doer.
'grew' is active (and past), so it cannot take 'by farmers' as the doer.

solution: Rice is grown by farmers in many parts of Asia.
'by farmers' names the doer, so the verb is passive; 'Rice' is singular, so 'is grown'.

questions.stem: The principal ____ the new library at the assembly yesterday morning.

explain.why: 'was opened' is passive and cannot be followed by the object 'the new library'; the principal did the opening.
'yesterday morning' is past, so the simple present 'opens' does not fit.
'has been opened' is passive and cannot take the object 'the new library'.

solution: The principal opened the new library at the assembly yesterday morning.
The subject 'The principal' does the action and the object 'the new library' follows, so the verb is active; 'yesterday morning' needs the simple past 'opened'.

questions.stem: The school fair ____ every year in November.

explain.why: 'is holding' is active, and the fair is not doing the holding.
'holds' is active, but the fair does not hold anything here; people hold the fair.
'hold' is a plural active form, but 'The school fair' is singular and receives the action.

solution: The school fair is held every year in November.
The fair receives the action and 'every year' shows a regular event, so use the simple present passive 'is held'.

questions.stem: Don't go in! The floor ____ at the moment.

explain.why: 'has been mopping' is active, but the floor does not do the mopping.
'at the moment' means now, so the past 'was mopped' does not fit.
'at the moment' shows the action is in progress, but 'is mopped' is the simple present passive for habits or facts.

solution: Don't go in! The floor is being mopped at the moment.
An action in progress now, done to the floor, takes the present continuous passive 'is being mopped'.

questions.stem: Our school's new science lab ____ since June.

explain.why: 'since June' links the past to now, so the simple present 'is used' does not fit.
'has been using' is active, but the lab does not use anything; it is used by pupils.
'since June' covers a period up to now, so the simple past 'was used' does not fit.

solution: Our school's new science lab has been used since June.
'since June' needs the present perfect, and the lab receives the action, so use the present perfect passive 'has been used'.

questions.stem: Ten new members ____ for the school choir so far.

explain.why: 'have been choosing' is active, but the members are the ones being chosen.
'so far' links the past to now, so the simple past 'were chosen' does not fit.
'Ten new members' is plural, so 'has been chosen' does not agree.

solution: Ten new members have been chosen for the school choir so far.
'so far' needs the present perfect and the members receive the action, so use 'have been chosen' (plural subject).

questions.stem: The litter must ____ before the principal's visit tomorrow.

explain.why: 'clear' is active, but the litter cannot clear itself; it is cleared by someone.
'be clearing' is active continuous, but the litter does not do the clearing.
'have cleared' is active, and the litter is not the one doing the clearing.

solution: The litter must be cleared before the principal's visit tomorrow.
After the modal 'must', the passive is 'be' + past participle: 'must be cleared'.

questions.stem: Several cars ____ in the car park last night, but nobody knows who did it.

explain.why: 'have damaged' is active and clashes with 'last night'; the cars were the ones harmed.
'were damaging' is active, but the cars did not do the damaging.
'damaged' is active and would need an object after it, but none follows; the cars received the damage.

solution: Several cars were damaged in the car park last night, but nobody knows who did it.
The cars receive the action and the doer is unknown, so use the agentless simple past passive 'were damaged'.

questions.stem: The results ____ at the end of the week.

explain.why: 'will be announcing' is active continuous, but the results are not the ones announcing.
'have announced' is active and past-linked, but 'at the end of the week' is future.
'will announce' is active, but results cannot announce anything; they are announced by the school.

solution: The results will be announced at the end of the week.
The results receive the action and the time is future, so use the future passive 'will be announced'.

questions.stem: The cleaners ____ the floor when the bell rang.

explain.why: 'had been mopped' is passive and cannot take the object 'the floor'.
'were mopped' is passive and cannot take the object 'the floor'; the cleaners did the mopping.
'was mopped' is passive and does not agree with the plural 'cleaners'.

solution: The cleaners were mopping the floor when the bell rang.
The cleaners do the action and 'the floor' is the object, so the verb is active; an action in progress when the bell rang takes the past continuous 'were mopping'.

questions.stem: By the time we arrived, all the tickets ____.

explain.why: 'we arrived' is past, so the future perfect 'will have been sold' does not fit.
'By the time we arrived' is in the past, so the present perfect 'have been sold' does not fit.
'all the tickets' is plural, so 'was sold' does not agree.

solution: By the time we arrived, all the tickets had been sold.
'By the time we arrived' (past) needs the past perfect for an earlier action; the tickets receive the action, so 'had been sold'.

questions.stem: The suspect ____ by the police at Changi Airport yesterday.

explain.why: 'yesterday' is a finished time, so the present perfect passive does not fit.
'was arresting' is active, but the suspect did not do the arresting.
'arrested' is active, but 'by the police' names the doer, so the suspect must be the receiver.

solution: The suspect was arrested by the police at Changi Airport yesterday.
'by the police' names the doer and 'yesterday' is past, so use the simple past passive 'was arrested'.

questions.stem: Tickets for the school concert ____ online from tomorrow.

explain.why: 'can have bought' is active and past-looking, but 'from tomorrow' is future.
'can buy' is active, but tickets cannot buy anything; people buy them.
'can be buying' is active continuous, and tickets are not doing the buying.

solution: Tickets for the school concert can be bought online from tomorrow.
After the modal 'can', the passive is 'be' + past participle: 'can be bought'.

questions.stem: The old school hall needs ____ before the concert.

explain.why: 'to be repairing' is active continuous, but the hall is not doing the repairing.
'to have repaired' is active perfect, and it does not make the hall the receiver of the repair.
'to repair' is active, but the hall does not repair anything; it receives the repair.

solution: The old school hall needs to be repaired before the concert.
The hall receives the action, so the passive infinitive 'to be repaired' follows 'needs'.

questions.stem: The new cafeteria is said ____ by a famous chef.

explain.why: 'to be designing' is active, but the cafeteria did not do the designing.
'to have been designing' is active continuous, but the cafeteria is not the designer.
'to have designed' is active, but 'by a famous chef' names the designer, so the cafeteria receives the action.

solution: The new cafeteria is said to have been designed by a famous chef.
The design was done earlier and the cafeteria receives it, so use the perfect passive infinitive 'to have been designed'.

questions.stem: Mum had the broken tap ____ by a plumber yesterday.

explain.why: 'had' + object is followed by the base form or a past participle, not by 'to fix'.
'fixing' would mean the tap was doing the fixing; the tap receives the action.
in 'had + object + base form' the object does the action, but the tap does not fix itself; 'by a plumber' needs the past participle.

solution: Mum had the broken tap fixed by a plumber yesterday.
'have + object + past participle' means someone else does the action to the object: 'had the tap fixed'.

questions.stem: Mei Ling was delighted about ____ the lead role by the drama teacher.

explain.why: 'giving' is active, which would make Mei Ling the giver; 'by the drama teacher' shows she received the role.
'about' is a preposition here, so the verb takes an -ing form, and 'to give' is also active.
'having given' is active, which would make Mei Ling the giver.

solution: Mei Ling was delighted about being given the lead role by the drama teacher.
After the preposition 'about' use an -ing form, and Mei Ling receives the role, so the passive gerund 'being given'.

questions.stem: Nobody enjoys ____ by the teacher in front of the whole class.

explain.why: 'scolding' is active, but 'by the teacher' shows the person is the one scolded.
'enjoy' is followed by an -ing form, not a to-infinitive.
'enjoy' does not take a to-infinitive, and 'to scold' is active.

solution: Nobody enjoys being scolded by the teacher in front of the whole class.
'enjoy' is followed by an -ing form, and the person receives the scolding, so the passive gerund 'being scolded'.

questions.stem: The temple is believed ____ over 200 years ago.

explain.why: 'to have been building' is active continuous, but the temple is not the builder.
'over 200 years ago' refers to a time before now, so the present infinitive 'to be built' does not fit.
'to have built' is active, but a temple does not build itself.

solution: The temple is believed to have been built over 200 years ago.
An earlier event that the temple receives needs the perfect passive infinitive 'to have been built'.

questions.stem: The school ____ that the concert has been cancelled.

explain.why: 'is announced' is passive and cannot take the 'that' clause as its object.
'was announced' is passive and cannot take the 'that' clause as its object.
'has been announced' is passive and cannot be followed by the object clause 'that the concert has been cancelled'; the school is the one announcing.

solution: The school has announced that the concert has been cancelled.
The school does the announcing and 'that the concert has been cancelled' is the object, so the verb is active: 'has announced'.

questions.stem: By 2030, many more HDB flats ____ in Punggol.

explain.why: 'By 2030' is in the future, so the past perfect 'had been built' does not fit.
'would have been built' refers to an unreal past, but 'By 2030' is a real future deadline.
'will have built' is active, but flats do not build themselves.

solution: By 2030, many more HDB flats will have been built in Punggol.
'By 2030' (a future deadline) takes the future perfect, and the flats receive the action, so 'will have been built'.

questions.stem: I am looking forward to ____ to the Science Olympiad.

explain.why: 'to' is a preposition in 'look forward to', so it takes an -ing form, not the base form.
'having invited' is active and past-looking, but the speaker looks forward to receiving an invitation.
'inviting' is active and would need an object; here the speaker is the one who receives the invitation.

solution: I am looking forward to being invited to the Science Olympiad.
'look forward to' takes an -ing form because 'to' is a preposition, and the speaker receives the invitation, so 'being invited'.

questions.stem:
Yesterday, Daniel said, "I am too tired to play." (He is fine today.)
Yesterday, Daniel said that he ____ too tired to play.

explain.why: 'he' is singular, so 'were' does not agree.
he spoke yesterday and is fine today, so the reported verb is shifted back; 'is' would put the tiredness in the present.
he described how he felt then, not a future state, so 'will be' is wrong.

solution: Yesterday, Daniel said that he was too tired to play.
The state is over and the report is about the past, so 'am' shifts back to 'was'.

questions.stem:
Last Monday, Alicia said, "I will visit my grandma tomorrow."
Last Monday, Alicia said that she would visit her grandma ____.

explain.why: 'yesterday' points backwards, but the visit was planned for the day after she spoke.
'the day before' points backwards, but the visit was planned for the day after she spoke.
'tomorrow' would point to the day after the reporter speaks; the report is about the day after last Monday.

solution: Last Monday, Alicia said that she would visit her grandma the next day.
In reported speech about a past occasion, 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day' (or 'the following day').

questions.stem:
Mrs Tan asked Kai, "Where do you live?"
Mrs Tan asked Kai where ____.

explain.why: a reported question keeps statement order, so the question form 'did he live' is wrong.
the subject 'he' must come before the verb in a reported question.
a reported question keeps statement order, so the question form 'does he live' is wrong.

solution: Mrs Tan asked Kai where he lived.
A reported question uses statement word order (subject + verb) with the tense shifted back: 'where he lived'.

questions.stem:
"Please sit down," the teacher said to us.
The teacher ____ us to sit down.

explain.why: 'say' is not followed by a person and a to-infinitive; the pattern 'told us to sit' is needed.
'talk' is not used with a person object plus a to-infinitive.
'speak' is not used with a person object plus a to-infinitive.

solution: The teacher told us to sit down.
'tell + person + to-infinitive' reports an instruction; 'say' cannot take that pattern.

questions.stem:
Yesterday, the driver said, "The bus will arrive soon." (It arrived five minutes later.)
Yesterday, the driver said that the bus ____ soon.

explain.why: the driver spoke yesterday and the bus has already arrived, so 'will' is shifted back to 'would'.
'would have arrived' is an unreal past, but the bus really did arrive later.
'arrived' says the arrival had happened, but he spoke before the bus came.

solution: Yesterday, the driver said that the bus would arrive soon.
In reported speech about a past occasion, 'will' shifts back to 'would'.

questions.stem:
Last year, Priya said, "I can't swim." (She has learnt since then.)
Last year, Priya said that she ____ swim.

explain.why: she has learnt to swim since then, so 'can't' would still be reported as true; the report shifts back.
'wouldn't' is the shift of 'won't', not 'can't'.
'may not' changes the meaning from lack of ability to possibility.

solution: Last year, Priya said that she couldn't swim.
In reported speech, 'can't' shifts back to 'couldn't'.

questions.stem:
"Do you want some water?" Aunty asked me.
Aunty asked me ____ I wanted some water.

explain.why: 'that' introduces a reported statement, not a yes/no question.
a reported question does not use 'do' as a link word; the joining word is 'if' or 'whether'.
'what' asks for a thing, but the original question could be answered yes or no.

solution: Aunty asked me if I wanted some water.
A yes/no question is reported with 'if' (or 'whether') and statement word order.

questions.stem:
"Don't run along the corridor," the prefect told us.
The prefect told us ____ along the corridor.

explain.why: 'didn't run' is a past statement, not a reported command.
a reported command uses the to-infinitive; 'don't run' keeps the original direct form.
after 'told us' the verb needs 'to', so 'not run' is incomplete.

solution: The prefect told us not to run along the corridor.
A negative command is reported as 'told + person + not to + verb'.

questions.stem:
On Friday, Mum said, "I bought these mooncakes yesterday."
On Friday, Mum said that she ____ those mooncakes the day before.

explain.why: 'would buy' looks forward, but 'the day before' is earlier.
the report is about a Friday statement, so the past simple shifts back to the past perfect, not the present perfect.
'was buying' would mean the buying was in progress, but she said the buying was finished.

solution: On Friday, Mum said that she had bought those mooncakes the day before.
'yesterday' becomes 'the day before' and the past simple 'bought' shifts back to 'had bought'.

questions.stem:
Last week, the residents asked, "When will the lift be repaired?" (It was repaired the next day.)
The residents asked when the lift ____.

explain.why: 'would repair' is active, but the lift receives the repair.
'had been repaired' says the repair was already done, but the question was about a future time.
the repair has already happened and the question was asked last week, so 'will' is shifted back to 'would'.

solution: The residents asked when the lift would be repaired.
'will be repaired' shifts back to 'would be repaired' in a reported question.

questions.stem:
"I'm sorry I broke your pencil box," said Jia Wei to Ken.
Jia Wei ____ for breaking Ken's pencil box.

explain.why: 'complained' needs 'about', and Jia Wei was saying sorry, not blaming anyone.
'suggested' does not fit 'for breaking'; Jia Wei was saying sorry, not offering an idea.
'refused' takes a to-infinitive and contradicts the apology.

solution: Jia Wei apologised for breaking Ken's pencil box.
'I'm sorry' is reported with 'apologised for + -ing'.

questions.stem:
"Let's have a picnic at East Coast Park," said Wei Xin.
Wei Xin ____ having a picnic at East Coast Park.

explain.why: 'complained' needs 'about', and 'Let's' is an idea, not a complaint.
'promised' takes a to-infinitive, not '-ing', and 'Let's' is an idea, not a promise.
'insisted' needs 'on' before 'having', and 'Let's' is a gentle idea, not a demand.

solution: Wei Xin suggested having a picnic at East Coast Park.
'Let's ...' is reported with 'suggested + -ing'.

questions.stem:
Last year, Siti said, "I was late because the bus broke down."
Siti said that she was late because the bus ____ down.

explain.why: 'will break' is future, but the breakdown had already happened.
the report is about last year, so the past simple shifts back to the past perfect.
'would break' looks forward, but the breakdown was the reason for being late, so it came earlier.

solution: Siti said that she was late because the bus had broken down.
The earlier action 'broke down' shifts back to the past perfect 'had broken down'.

questions.stem:
"Shall I carry your bag?" Daniel asked Mrs Lee.
Daniel ____ to carry Mrs Lee's bag.

explain.why: 'Shall I ...?' is a polite offer, not a demand.
'refused to carry' would mean he would not carry it, which is the opposite of the offer.
'reminded' needs a person object before 'to', so 'reminded to carry' is incomplete.

solution: Daniel offered to carry Mrs Lee's bag.
'Shall I ...?' offering help is reported with 'offered to + verb'.

questions.stem:
"I will help you," Jun Wei said to me.
Jun Wei ____ me that he would help.

explain.why: 'said' cannot take a person directly; it would need 'said to me'.
'spoke' is not followed by a person and a 'that' clause.
'explained' needs 'to me', so 'explained me that' is wrong.

solution: Jun Wei told me that he would help.
'tell' takes a person object directly before a 'that' clause.

questions.stem:
That evening, the usher asked us, "How long have you been waiting?"
The usher asked us how long we ____.

explain.why: a reported question uses statement order, so 'had we been waiting' is wrong.
the question was asked in the past, so the present perfect continuous shifts back to the past perfect continuous.
'would be waiting' looks forward, but the usher asked about waiting already done.

solution: That evening, the usher asked us how long we had been waiting.
The present perfect continuous shifts back to the past perfect continuous, in statement order.

questions.stem:
"Give me your ticket," said Mr Lau, the conductor, to Raj.
Mr Lau told Raj to give ____ his ticket.

explain.why: 'me' referred to Mr Lau when he spoke; the reporter is a different person, so 'me' is wrong.
Mr Lau is one person, so the plural 'them' does not fit.
'you' referred to Raj when spoken; in a report about Raj, this becomes 'him', and the receiver of the ticket is Mr Lau.

solution: Mr Lau told Raj to give him his ticket.
'me' (Mr Lau speaking) becomes 'him' in the report.

questions.stem:
"I didn't take your eraser," said Hui Min.
Hui Min denied ____ the eraser.

explain.why: 'deny' is followed by an -ing form, so the bare 'take' is wrong.
'deny' is followed by an -ing form, not a to-infinitive.
'took' is the simple past; after 'having' the past participle 'taken' is needed.

solution: Hui Min denied taking the eraser.
'deny' is followed by an -ing form.

questions.stem:
"You copied my answers!" Ming said to Jo.
Ming ____ Jo of copying his answers.

explain.why: 'warned' does not fit; Ming was charging Jo with something already done, not warning about a danger.
'blame' is followed by 'for', not 'of'.
'criticise' is followed by 'for', not 'of'.

solution: Ming accused Jo of copying his answers.
'accuse someone of + -ing' reports a charge of wrongdoing.

questions.stem:
"You should see a doctor," Mum said to me.
Mum advised me ____ a doctor.

explain.why: 'advise + person' is followed by a to-infinitive, not an -ing form.
'advised me should see' is ungrammatical; 'advise + person' needs a to-infinitive.
'advise + person' needs 'to' before the verb.

solution: Mum advised me to see a doctor.
'advise + person + to-infinitive' reports advice.

questions.stem:
Vik said, "Had I known, I would have come."
Vik said that if he ____ known, he would have come.

explain.why: 'did known' is not a verb form; the past perfect 'had known' is needed.
'if he has known' is a present perfect, which does not fit an unreal past condition.
'if he have known' is ungrammatical; the subject 'he' with a past perfect needs 'had'.

solution: Vik said that if he had known, he would have come.
A past unreal condition keeps 'if + had + past participle' in reported speech.

questions.stem:
Last Saturday, Su Lin asked Joel, "Are you coming to the party or not?"
Su Lin asked Joel whether ____ to the party or not.

explain.why: 'he' is singular, so 'were' does not agree.
a reported question uses statement order, so 'was he coming' is wrong.
'he coming' has no finite verb after 'whether'.

solution: Su Lin asked Joel whether he was coming to the party or not.
'are coming' shifts back to 'was coming', in statement order after 'whether'.

questions.stem:
"I'll definitely finish the model by Monday," Aaron said.
Aaron ____ to finish the model by Monday.

explain.why: 'admitted' means owning up to something done, not a plan for the future.
'regretted' means feeling sorry, and does not fit a promise.
'denied' takes an -ing form and means saying 'no' to a claim.

solution: Aaron promised to finish the model by Monday.
'I'll definitely ...' is a promise, reported with 'promised to + verb'.

questions.stem:
"Don't forget to bring your passes," Mr Lee said to us.
Mr Lee ____ us to bring our passes.

explain.why: 'remembered' means recalling something himself; it does not take 'us to bring'.
'recalled' means bringing something back to mind, and it does not take 'us to bring'.
'forgot' means he failed to remember, which is the opposite of what he said.

solution: Mr Lee reminded us to bring our passes.
'Don't forget to ...' is reported with 'reminded + person + to-infinitive'.

questions.stem: Kai swam in the pool, and so ____ his sister.

explain.why: 'swam' is the simple past, so the echo uses 'did', not 'had'.
'swam' is an ordinary verb, so the echo uses 'did', not a form of 'be'.
'swam' is past, so the matching auxiliary is 'did', not present 'does'.

solution: Kai swam in the pool, and so did his sister.
'so + auxiliary + subject' echoes the first clause; the simple past 'swam' is echoed by 'did'.

questions.stem: "I can't speak Malay." "Neither ____ I."

explain.why: 'can't speak' is echoed with 'can', not with a form of 'be'.
'Neither' is already negative, so 'can't' makes a double negative.
'can't' is echoed with the same modal 'can', not 'do'.

solution: "I can't speak Malay." "Neither can I."
'Neither + auxiliary + subject' agrees with a negative statement; the auxiliary repeats the modal 'can'.

questions.stem: My brother doesn't eat durian, nor ____ my father.

explain.why: 'doesn't eat' is echoed with 'does', not a form of 'be'.
'doesn't eat' is present simple, so the echo is 'does', not 'will'.
'my father' is singular, so 'do' does not agree; 'does' is needed.

solution: My brother doesn't eat durian, nor does my father.
'nor + auxiliary + subject' echoes a negative; 'doesn't' is echoed by 'does' with a singular subject.

questions.stem: Not only ____ the first prize, but she also broke the school record.

explain.why: inversion uses an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb 'won' alone.
after 'Not only' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'she won' does not invert.
'she did' has the subject first, but after 'Not only' the auxiliary must come first.

solution: Not only did she win the first prize, but she also broke the school record.
A sentence starting with 'Not only' inverts: auxiliary + subject + base verb ('did she win').

questions.stem: No sooner had we reached the bus stop ____ it began to rain.

explain.why: 'No sooner' is paired with 'than'; 'when' belongs with 'Hardly' or 'Scarcely'.
'then' is a time adverb and cannot link the two clauses here.
'that' does not complete 'No sooner'; the partner word is 'than'.

solution: No sooner had we reached the bus stop than it began to rain.
'No sooner' + past perfect is completed by 'than'.

questions.stem: Hardly had I sat down ____ the bell rang.

explain.why: 'Hardly' is paired with 'when', not 'that'.
'while' means 'during the time that', but the bell rang right after sitting down; 'Hardly' is paired with 'when'.
'then' is an adverb and cannot link the two clauses.

solution: Hardly had I sat down when the bell rang.
'Hardly' + past perfect is completed by 'when'.

questions.stem: Only after the guests left ____ the mess in the hall.

explain.why: after 'Only after ...', the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'we noticed' does not invert.
inversion needs an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb alone.
the subject 'we' is before the auxiliary, but 'Only after' needs 'did' first.

solution: Only after the guests left did we notice the mess in the hall.
A sentence starting with 'Only after ...' inverts: 'did we notice'.

questions.stem: Never ____ such a delicious laksa before.

explain.why: after 'Never' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'I have eaten' does not invert.
inversion uses an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb alone.
after 'Never' at the start the sentence inverts, and 'before' needs the perfect form.

solution: Never have I eaten such a delicious laksa before.
A sentence starting with 'Never' inverts; 'before' with an experience takes the present perfect: 'have I eaten'.

questions.stem: "I can ride a bike." "So ____ I."

explain.why: 'can ride' is echoed with 'can', not with a form of 'be'.
'can ride' is echoed with the same modal 'can', not 'do'.
'can ride' is echoed with 'can', not 'have'.

solution: "I can ride a bike." "So can I."
'So + auxiliary + subject' agrees with a positive statement; the auxiliary repeats the modal 'can'.

questions.stem: Not only does the library lend books, ____ it also offers free workshops.

explain.why: 'or' gives a choice, but the library does both things.
'Not only' is paired with 'but (also)', not 'so'.
'then' is an adverb, and 'Not only' needs the conjunction 'but'.

solution: Not only does the library lend books, but it also offers free workshops.
'Not only ... but also ...' links two things done by the same subject.

questions.stem: Hardly ____ the shop when the fire alarm rang.

explain.why: 'Hardly ... when' uses the past perfect 'had entered', not 'did enter'.
the alarm rang in the past, so the past perfect 'had we entered' is needed, not 'have'.
after 'Hardly' at the start, 'had' comes before the subject; 'we had' does not invert.

solution: Hardly had we entered the shop when the fire alarm rang.
'Hardly' at the start inverts the past perfect: 'had + subject + past participle'.

questions.stem: No sooner ____ off the lights than the baby started to cry.

explain.why: after 'No sooner' at the start, 'had' comes before the subject; 'I had' does not invert.
'No sooner ... than' uses the past perfect 'had switched', not 'did switch'.
the baby started to cry in the past, so the past perfect 'had I switched' is needed.

solution: No sooner had I switched off the lights than the baby started to cry.
'No sooner' at the start inverts the past perfect: 'had + subject + past participle'.

questions.stem: Su Ling waited nervously. Only after the results were announced ____ how well she had done.

explain.why: after 'Only after ...' the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'she realised' does not invert.
the subject is before 'did', but 'Only after' needs 'did' first.
inversion needs an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb alone.

solution: Su Ling waited nervously. Only after the results were announced did she realise how well she had done.
'Only after ...' at the start inverts the main clause: 'did + subject + base verb'.

questions.stem: "Alicia didn't go to the concert." "Neither ____ Wen Hui."

explain.why: 'didn't go' is echoed with 'did', not a form of 'be'.
'didn't go' is past, so the echo uses 'did', not present 'does'.
'Neither' is already negative, so 'didn't' makes a double negative.

solution: "Alicia didn't go to the concert." "Neither did Wen Hui."
'Neither + auxiliary + subject' echoes a negative; 'didn't go' is echoed by 'did'.

questions.stem: Scarcely ____ the stage when the audience began to clap.

explain.why: the audience clapped in the past, so the past perfect 'had she reached' is needed.
after 'Scarcely' at the start, 'had' comes before the subject; 'she had' does not invert.
'Scarcely ... when' uses the past perfect 'had reached', not 'did reach'.

solution: Scarcely had she reached the stage when the audience began to clap.
'Scarcely' at the start inverts the past perfect: 'had + subject + past participle'.

questions.stem: Not until the guests arrived ____ the cake.

explain.why: after 'Not until ...' the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'we cut' does not invert.
inversion needs an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb alone.
the subject is before 'did', but 'Not until' needs 'did' first.

solution: Not until the guests arrived did we cut the cake.
'Not until ...' at the start inverts the main clause: 'did + subject + base verb'.

questions.stem: So heavy ____ that the match was cancelled.

explain.why: the match was cancelled in the past, so the past 'was the rain' is needed.
after 'So heavy' at the start, the verb comes before the subject; 'the rain was' does not invert.
'be' does not take 'do'; 'did the rain' has no main verb.

solution: So heavy was the rain that the match was cancelled.
'So + adjective' at the start inverts the verb 'be' before the subject: 'was the rain'.

questions.stem: Seldom ____ such a large crowd at this hawker centre.

explain.why: inversion needs an auxiliary before the subject, not the main verb alone.
the subject is before 'do', but 'Seldom' needs 'do' first.
after 'Seldom' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'we see' does not invert.

solution: Seldom do we see such a large crowd at this hawker centre.
'Seldom' at the start inverts the main clause: 'do + subject + base verb'.

questions.stem: "I wasn't at the meeting." "Neither ____ I."

explain.why: 'wasn't' is past, so the echo is 'was', not present 'am'.
'wasn't' is a form of 'be', so the echo uses 'was', not 'did'.
'I' takes 'was', not 'were'.

solution: "I wasn't at the meeting." "Neither was I."
'Neither + auxiliary + subject' echoes a negative; 'wasn't' is echoed by 'was'.

questions.stem: "Mum doesn't like spicy food." "Neither ____ Dad."

explain.why: 'doesn't like' is echoed with 'does', not a form of 'be'.
'Dad' is singular, so 'do' does not agree; 'does' is needed.
'Neither' is already negative, so 'doesn't' makes a double negative.

solution: "Mum doesn't like spicy food." "Neither does Dad."
'Neither + auxiliary + subject' echoes a negative; 'doesn't like' is echoed by 'does' with a singular subject.

questions.stem: Not only the students but also the teacher ____ finished the project.

explain.why: with 'Not only ... but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the teacher', which is singular.
'is finished the project' is ungrammatical; the perfect needs 'has finished'.
'are finished the project' is ungrammatical; the perfect needs 'has finished'.

solution: Not only the students but also the teacher has finished the project.
With 'Not only ... but also ...' the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it: 'the teacher' takes 'has'.

questions.stem: Only by practising every day ____ the violin well.

explain.why: 'can' is already an auxiliary, so 'do' is not added.
after 'Only by ...' the modal comes before the subject; 'you can play' does not invert.
the subject must follow the modal, not come after the main verb.

solution: Only by practising every day can you play the violin well.
'Only by ...' at the start inverts the main clause: modal + subject + base verb.

questions.stem: ____ I known about the road closure, I would have taken the MRT.

explain.why: 'Would I known' is ungrammatical; 'would' needs a base verb.
'Have I known' does not form an unreal past condition; the past perfect needs 'Had'.
'Did I known' is ungrammatical; 'Did' takes the base form.

solution: Had I known about the road closure, I would have taken the MRT.
'Had + subject + past participle' replaces 'If I had known' in a past unreal condition.

questions.stem: "Siti has never been late." "Nor ____ Hui Min."

explain.why: 'Hui Min' is singular, so 'have' does not agree.
'has been' is echoed with 'has', not 'does'.
'has been' is a present perfect, so the echo uses 'has', not 'is'.

solution: "Siti has never been late." "Nor has Hui Min."
'Nor + auxiliary + subject' echoes a negative; 'has been' is echoed by 'has'.

questions.stem: Not only did the volunteers clean the beach, but they ____ the old signboards.

explain.why: after 'did' in the first part, the second part needs a past verb 'repaired', not the base form.
'had repair' is not a verb form; the simple past 'repaired' is needed.
'repairing' without 'were' is not a finite past verb.

solution: Not only did the volunteers clean the beach, but they also repaired the old signboards.
In the 'but' part of 'Not only ... but also', the verb is in the normal order and in the same past tense: 'also repaired'.

questions.stem: Only after the final bell had rung ____ the classroom.

explain.why: after 'Only after ...' the auxiliary comes before the subject; 'the pupils left' does not invert.
the subject is before 'did', but 'Only after' needs 'did' first.
the leaving came after the bell, so the main clause uses the simple past 'did ... leave', not the past perfect.

solution: Only after the final bell had rung did the pupils leave the classroom.
'Only after ...' at the start inverts the main clause: 'did + subject + base verb'.

questions.stem: Ben missed the start of the briefing. Not only ____ late, but he also forgot his notes.

explain.why: 'did' is the wrong auxiliary for 'be', and the subject is also before it.
after 'Not only' at the start the verb comes before the subject; 'he was' does not invert.
'be' does not take 'do'; 'did he late' has no main verb.

solution: Ben missed the start of the briefing. Not only was he late, but he also forgot his notes.
'Not only' at the start inverts 'be' before the subject: 'was he'.

questions.stem: At no time during last term ____ the pupils allowed to use phones in class.

explain.why: 'the pupils' is plural, so 'was' does not agree.
'have the pupils allowed' needs 'been' to be passive.
'last term' is past, so 'are' does not fit.

solution: At no time during last term were the pupils allowed to use phones in class.
'At no time' at the start inverts: verb 'be' before the subject, here past and plural: 'were the pupils'.

questions.stem: Our class ____ a science project last Friday.

explain.why: 'last Friday' is a finished past time, but 'completes' is simple present.
'last Friday' is already past, so the future 'will complete' cannot be used.
'is completing' is present continuous, but 'last Friday' needs the simple past.

solution: Our class completed a science project last Friday.
'last Friday' marks a finished time in the past, so use the simple past 'completed'.

questions.stem: Look! The pupils ____ towards the school bus.

explain.why: 'Look!' shows the action is happening now, so past continuous 'were running' is wrong.
'Look!' points to an action happening now, which needs the present continuous, not the simple present for habits.
'Look!' signals something happening now, so the simple past 'ran' does not fit.

solution: Look! The pupils are running towards the school bus.
'Look!' signals an action in progress now, so use the present continuous 'are running'.

questions.stem: My father ____ to work by MRT every morning.

explain.why: 'every morning' with the present 'My father' is a habit now, not a finished past event.
'every morning' shows a habit, which uses the simple present, not the present continuous.
'has gone' means he has left and is not here; it does not describe a daily habit.

solution: My father goes to work by MRT every morning.
'every morning' shows a habit, so use the simple present 'goes'.

questions.stem: Ben ____ his lunch when the fire alarm rang.

explain.why: 'were' is plural, but the subject 'Ben' is singular.
'eats' is simple present, but 'rang' puts the story in the past.
'rang' is past, so the action in progress at that time must be past continuous, not 'is eating'.

solution: Ben was eating his lunch when the fire alarm rang.
A longer past action interrupted by a shorter one uses the past continuous: 'was eating' when the alarm rang.

questions.stem: By the time we arrived, the film ____ already started.

explain.why: 'did' must be followed by the base form 'start', but the sentence has 'started'.
'the film' is singular, so 'have' does not agree; the past perfect also needs 'had'.
'arrived' is past, so the earlier action needs past perfect 'had started', not present perfect 'has started'.

solution: By the time we arrived, the film had already started.
'By the time we arrived' needs the past perfect 'had started' for the earlier action.

questions.stem: Tomorrow, our teacher ____ us the results of the spelling test.

explain.why: 'has given' is present perfect and cannot go with the future time 'Tomorrow'.
'Tomorrow' points to the future, so the simple past 'gave' is wrong.
'was giving' is past continuous, but 'Tomorrow' needs a future form.

solution: Tomorrow, our teacher will give us the results of the spelling test.
'Tomorrow' needs the future 'will give'.

questions.stem: Aisha ____ in this HDB block since she was born.

explain.why: 'since she was born' links the past to now, so the present perfect 'has lived' is needed, not the simple past.
'since' with a starting point needs a perfect tense; simple present 'lives' does not fit.
'is living' is present continuous and does not combine with 'since' to show a period up to now.

solution: Aisha has lived in this HDB block since she was born.
'since' + a past starting point takes the present perfect 'has lived'.

questions.stem: ____ you finished your homework yet?

explain.why: 'Did' must be followed by the base form 'finish', but the sentence has 'finished'.
'Will' must be followed by the base form 'finish', but the sentence has 'finished'.
'you' takes 'have', not 'has'.

solution: Have you finished your homework yet?
'yet' with 'finished' needs the present perfect, so 'Have you finished'.

questions.stem: The bus ____ by the time Wei Ling reached the stop.

explain.why: 'reached' is past, so the earlier action needs past perfect, not present perfect 'has left'.
'is leaving' is present continuous, which clashes with the past 'reached'.
'would leave' looks forward from the past; here the bus left before she reached the stop.

solution: The bus had already left by the time Wei Ling reached the stop.
'By the time' + simple past takes the past perfect for the earlier event: 'had already left'.

questions.stem: Since the new library opened, the number of visitors ____ steadily.

explain.why: 'Since the library opened' covers a period up to now, so past continuous 'was rising' does not fit.
'since' needs a perfect tense; simple present continuous 'is rising' does not connect to the starting point.
'The number' is singular, so 'has' is needed, not 'have'.

solution: Since the new library opened, the number of visitors has been rising steadily.
'Since' + a past event needs the present perfect, and 'the number' is singular: 'has been rising'.

questions.stem: Mrs Tan ____ at this school for twenty years when she retired last month.

explain.why: 'for twenty years' before another past event needs a perfect form, not past continuous.
'would teach' does not show a completed period of twenty years before she retired.
'retired last month' is past, so present perfect continuous 'has been teaching' does not fit.

solution: Mrs Tan had been teaching at this school for twenty years when she retired last month.
A period lasting up to an earlier past moment uses the past perfect continuous: 'had been teaching'.

questions.stem: While I ____ for the bus, it started to rain heavily.

explain.why: 'would wait' does not show an action in progress when the rain started.
'started' is past, so present perfect continuous 'have been waiting' clashes with it.
'started' is past, so simple present 'wait' is inconsistent.

solution: While I was waiting for the bus, it started to rain heavily.
'While' with a past interruption takes the past continuous 'was waiting'.

questions.stem: Ravi ____ his keys, so he could not enter the house.

explain.why: 'could not enter' is past, so the earlier loss needs 'had lost', not 'has lost'.
'was losing' describes a process, but the keys were already gone before he reached the door.
'loses' is simple present, but 'could not enter' is past.

solution: Ravi had lost his keys, so he could not enter the house.
The loss happened before 'could not enter', so use the past perfect 'had lost'.

questions.stem: How long ____ you been learning the violin?

explain.why: 'will been' is ungrammatical; 'been learning' needs 'have' before it.
'you' takes 'have', not 'has'.
'did' cannot be followed by 'been learning'; 'been' needs 'have' before it.

solution: How long have you been learning the violin?
'been learning' is present perfect continuous, so the auxiliary is 'have' after 'you'.

questions.stem: I ____ my cousin tomorrow, so I cannot come for the CCA session.

explain.why: 'tomorrow' is in the future, so simple past 'visited' is wrong.
'tomorrow' needs a future form; present perfect 'have visited' is wrong.
'was visiting' is past, but the plan is for tomorrow.

solution: I am visiting my cousin tomorrow, so I cannot come for the CCA session.
A fixed plan for the future can use the present continuous: 'am visiting ... tomorrow'.

questions.stem: My brother ____ the guitar for three years now.

explain.why: 'for three years now' shows a period up to now, so simple present 'plays' does not fit.
'now' links to the present, so past perfect 'had played' is wrong.
'My brother' is singular, so 'has' is needed, not 'have'.

solution: My brother has been playing the guitar for three years now.
'for three years now' needs the present perfect continuous 'has been playing'.

questions.stem: By next June, Kai Wen ____ in this choir for four years.

explain.why: 'By next June' is future; 'had been singing' belongs to the past.
'would sing' cannot express the total length of time reached by next June.
'would have been singing' is an unreal past form and does not give the real total reached by next June.

solution: By next June, Kai Wen will have been singing in this choir for four years.
'By next June' + a length of time takes the future perfect (continuous): 'will have been singing'.

questions.stem: The museum guide explained that the ship ____ in 1850 and had sailed to Singapore many times since.

explain.why: The ship did not do the building; it needs the passive 'was built'.
'in 1850' is a past date, and the clause after 'explained' is in the past, so 'is built' is inconsistent.
'in 1850' is a fixed past time, which cannot be used with the present perfect.

solution: The museum guide explained that the ship was built in 1850 and had sailed to Singapore many times since.
A ship is built by people, so the passive 'was built', with the past date 'in 1850'.

questions.stem: Although it ____ heavily since morning, the football match went on as planned.

explain.why: 'since morning' needs a perfect form; 'was raining' cannot take 'since'.
'since morning' cannot go with the simple past 'rained'.
'went on' is past, so present perfect continuous 'has been raining' is inconsistent.

solution: Although it had been raining heavily since morning, the football match went on as planned.
'since morning' before a past event ('went on') needs the past perfect continuous 'had been raining'.

questions.stem: The runner collapsed at the finish line because he ____ without stopping for two hours.

explain.why: 'runs' is simple present and clashes with 'collapsed'.
'collapsed' is past, so present perfect continuous 'has been running' does not match.
'is running' is present, but the whole sentence is in the past.

solution: The runner collapsed at the finish line because he had been running without stopping for two hours.
A long action before a past event takes the past perfect continuous: 'had been running'.

questions.stem: Next week, when the P6 pupils ____ their oral exam, they will take a short break.

explain.why: 'will' is not used inside a 'when' clause about the future.
'would finish' is a past-based form and does not fit 'Next week ... will take'.
After 'when' for a future event, the verb stays in a present form; 'will' is not used inside the clause.

solution: Next week, when the P6 pupils have finished their oral exam, they will take a short break.
After 'when' in a future sentence, use a present form; 'have finished' shows it is done first.

questions.stem: Whenever the haze got bad, my grandfather ____ the windows and switched on the air purifier.

explain.why: 'got' and 'switched' are past, so 'will close' is inconsistent.
A repeated habit in the past uses 'would', not past perfect, which shows an earlier action.
'would' must be followed by the base form 'close', not 'closed'.

solution: Whenever the haze got bad, my grandfather would close the windows and switched on the air purifier.
'Whenever ... got' describes a repeated past habit, so use 'would close'.

questions.stem: Jia Hui ____ the piano since Primary 3, and she is now preparing for her Grade 5 exam.

explain.why: 'since' needs the present perfect; simple present 'plays' cannot take 'since'.
'since Primary 3' and 'is now' need a perfect tense, not the simple past.
'is now preparing' is present, so past perfect 'had played' is inconsistent.

solution: Jia Hui has played the piano since Primary 3, and she is now preparing for her Grade 5 exam.
'since Primary 3' up to the present takes the present perfect 'has played'.

questions.stem: I wish I ____ more attention during yesterday's lesson.

explain.why: A wish about the past ('yesterday') needs the past perfect, not simple past.
'would pay' expresses a wish about the future, not a regret about yesterday.
'wish' is followed by a past form, not present perfect 'have paid'.

solution: I wish I had paid more attention during yesterday's lesson.
A wish about a past event takes the past perfect: 'I wish I had paid'.

questions.stem: It was only after the guests had left that Mum realised she ____ to buy dessert.

explain.why: 'was forgetting' shows a process, but the forgetting was a completed earlier event.
'would forget' looks forward; the forgetting happened before she realised.
'realised' is past, so present perfect 'has forgotten' is inconsistent.

solution: It was only after the guests had left that Mum realised she had forgotten to buy dessert.
The forgetting came before 'realised', so use the past perfect 'had forgotten'.

questions.stem: The school fair will be held ____ Saturday.

explain.why: 'at' is used for clock times and points, not for days of the week.
'by' means 'no later than', not the day on which an event is held.
'in' is used for months, years and parts of a day, not a named day.

solution: The school fair will be held on Saturday.
Days of the week take 'on': on Saturday.

questions.stem: The accident happened ____ midnight.

explain.why: 'by midnight' means 'before midnight', not the moment it happened.
'in' is used with longer periods such as 'in the morning', not an exact time.
'on' is used with days and dates, not with an exact time like midnight.

solution: The accident happened at midnight.
A point in time such as midnight takes 'at'.

questions.stem: She has been learning the piano ____ three years.

explain.why: 'during' needs a named period (during the holidays), not a number of years.
'since' needs a starting point such as 'Primary 3', but 'three years' is a length of time.
'at' cannot introduce a length of time.

solution: She has been learning the piano for three years.
A length of time ('three years') takes 'for'.

questions.stem: He has been absent ____ Monday.

explain.why: 'during' needs a named period or event, not a starting day like 'Monday'.
'at' is used for clock times, not for a starting day.
'for' needs a length of time such as 'three days', but 'Monday' is a starting point.

solution: He has been absent since Monday.
A starting point in time ('Monday') takes 'since'.

questions.stem: Wei Jie is very good ____ drawing.

explain.why: The adjective 'good' takes 'at' for a skill, not 'in'.
'good on' does not describe a skill.
'good with' is used for handling people or things, not for a skill like drawing.

solution: Wei Jie is very good at drawing.
'good at' + a skill or activity.

questions.stem: I am afraid ____ spiders.

explain.why: 'afraid to' needs a verb after it, not a noun like 'spiders'.
The adjective 'afraid' takes 'of', not 'from'.
'afraid for' means worried about someone's safety, not a fear of spiders.

solution: I am afraid of spiders.
'afraid of' + the thing feared.

questions.stem: Our team is responsible ____ keeping the classroom tidy.

explain.why: 'responsible' takes 'for' when it names the job, not 'of'.
'responsible with' is not the usual collocation for a duty.
'responsible to' means answerable to a person, not in charge of a task.

solution: Our team is responsible for keeping the classroom tidy.
'responsible for' + the duty.

questions.stem: I have been looking forward ____ the school camp.

explain.why: 'look forward on' is not an English phrase.
The phrase is 'look forward to', not 'look forward for'.
'look forward at' is not an English phrase.

solution: I have been looking forward to the school camp.
'look forward to' + a noun or gerund.

questions.stem: The hawker was fined ____ selling food without a licence.

explain.why: 'fined on' is not used for the offence.
'fined with' is not used for the offence.
'fined of' is not used; the reason for a fine takes 'for'.

solution: The hawker was fined for selling food without a licence.
'fined for' + the offence.

questions.stem: Please return the library books ____ next Monday.

explain.why: 'during' needs a period of time that something happens within, not a deadline day.
'on' names a day an event happens, and 'on next Monday' is not used; a deadline needs 'by'.
'until' is used for an action that continues up to a time, but returning is a one-time action with a deadline.

solution: Please return the library books by next Monday.
A deadline ('no later than next Monday') takes 'by'.

questions.stem: The cat hid ____ the sofa and the wall.

explain.why: 'among' is used for three or more things; here there are only two, the sofa and the wall.
'beside' means next to one thing, but the cat is in the gap between two.
'against' means pressed on something and does not fit two objects with 'and'.

solution: The cat hid between the sofa and the wall.
Two objects joined by 'and' take 'between'.

questions.stem: She cut the cake ____ a knife.

explain.why: 'through' means passing from one side to another, not using a tool.
'in' does not show the tool used.
'by' is used for means like 'by bus', not for a tool.

solution: She cut the cake with a knife.
A tool or instrument takes 'with'.

questions.stem: Ali insisted ____ paying for everyone's drinks at the hawker centre.

explain.why: 'insist' takes 'on' before a gerund, not 'to'.
'insist with' is not used in English.
'insist for' is not used in English.

solution: Ali insisted on paying for everyone's drinks at the hawker centre.
'insist on' + gerund.

questions.stem: Whether the school camp can go ahead after weeks of planning depends entirely ____ the weather.

explain.why: 'depend with' is not used in English.
'depend to' is not used in English.
'depend' takes 'on', not 'from'.

solution: Whether the school camp can go ahead after weeks of planning depends entirely on the weather.
'depend on' + the factor.

questions.stem: Despite the heavy rain, the volunteers carried on ____ clearing the drains.

explain.why: 'carry on for' is not used for continuing a task.
'carry on from' means continuing from a point, not continuing with a task.
'carry on by clearing' would mean the way they continued, not the same task.

solution: Despite the heavy rain, the volunteers carried on with clearing the drains.
'carry on with' + the task.

questions.stem: Instead ____ complaining about the long queue, Mei Xin chatted with the stallholder.

explain.why: The phrase is 'instead of', not 'instead for'.
The phrase is 'instead of', not 'instead to'.
The phrase is 'instead of', not 'instead from'.

solution: Instead of complaining about the long queue, Mei Xin chatted with the stallholder.
'instead of' + gerund.

questions.stem: I would like to apologise ____ keeping you waiting.

explain.why: 'apologise' takes 'for' before the reason, not 'of'.
